utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, good morning everyone. I note Mr. Pavkovic is not with us. Mr. Aleksic, I understand there will be a waiver to allow the proceedings to continue in his absence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Good morning. Yes, yes, it will arrive during the course of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Our next witness will be Danica Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document now being shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, and try to make yourself comfortable with the technology. You'll now be examined by Mr. Ivetic. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And with the number of exhibits that we have with this witness, I've prepared three binders of hard copies so to perhaps run things a little more smoothly. With Your Honour's leave, I would ask for the usher to hand the three binders to the witness and maybe if we can have the Office of the Prosecutor's representative look at it just to make sure that they're unmarked copies of the exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Judge Marinkovic. As you know, I'm Dan Ivetic. For purposes of the record could you please introduce yourself to everyone in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning to all in the courtroom. I am Danica Marinkovic. I live with my family in Belgrade, but I work in Kragujevac as a district court judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the record as well, could you give us a brief biography of your educational background since you've already given us your current residence.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I completed elementary and secondary school and graduated from university in Skoplje, where I lived until I got married. After I finished university I started working as a trainee at the court in Skoplje, and that is where I passed the bar exam after my internship, and after passing the bar exam I worked as a counsellor at the Supreme Court in Pristina. I worked there until 1984, and I started working on the 1st of September, 1976. From 1984 until the present day, I am a judge of the district court; however, as a judge of the district court in -- I worked as a judge of the district court in Pristina until 2004, and since the 1st of March, 2004, until the present day, I am a judge of the district court in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and I'm just waiting for the transcript to catch up with us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are these dates accurate, Mr. Ivetic, as a judge of the district court in Pristina until 2004?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Let me ask the witness to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Judge Marinkovic, the transcript reflects that you have been the -- you have worked as a judge of the district court in Pristina until 2004. Could you please explain that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I can. I was a judge of the district court in Pristina before the bombing and during the NATO bombing and after we were expelled from Pristina. However, in accordance with a ruling of the Supreme Court of Serbia in Belgrade, the courts from the territory of Kosovo and Metohija were temporarily relocated to the territory of the interior of Serbia until they returned to Kosovo. So the seat of my court was in Nis, so I continued working as a judge on the district court in Pristina but this was in Nis. On the 1st of March, 2004, by a decision of the president of the Supreme Court from Belgrade, I was sent to work temporarily in the district court in Kragujevac because they needed assistance. And since we judges from Kosovo and Metohija were temporarily unassigned, they offered that position to me, and I accepted and I started working there. I worked there by way of assistance for two years, and then after that in accordance with the law on judges on the basis of the council for the judiciary, I was taken over on a permanent basis by the district court of Kragujevac, and now I'm a judge of the district court in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I think that clears it up. And could you please tell us your ethnic background or ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, did you have an opportunity to complete a written statement as part of your preparations with the Defence team of Sreten Lukic to be used as part of your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like with the usher's assistance to show you Exhibit 6D1495, a hard copy of your statement. And, Judge Marinkovic, once you receive this if you could please take a moment to review the same and let us know if this is indeed the written statement that you've prepared and which you read in full before signing and affirming.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my written statement that I read and signed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if I were to ask you questions on the same topics as covered in your written statement today, would you give the same answers under oath as are set forth in the statement?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask for the statement 6D1495 to be admitted into evidence as we have both an English and an original Serbian copy in e-court under that number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Judge Marinkovic, can you tell us, please, during the time you spent living in Pristina, what were your observations of how people of different ethnicities interacted as well as your own personal experiences in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: While I lived in Pristina, that is -- that was from 1976 until June 1999, when we were expelled from Pristina, relations among people of different ethnic backgrounds were as normal as possible. The usual thing, people had contacts, socialised, helped each other out. I can say on the basis of my personal experience that I had acquaintances of Albanian ethnicity in the apartment building where we lived. We had neighbours with whom we had good neighbourly relations. We visited each other. I had an Albanian mechanic who helped me maintain my car. I had a dress-maker who was close to the courthouse where I worked, and I went to him regularly for his services, although his brother who had worked at a cashier for the public utilities, waterworks and sewage, he was a crime suspect and I carried out an investigation in relation to that person, his brother, but I did my work professionally and even after the investigation of this case was completed our relationship remained the same. In the building where I lived, there was a man who owned a small store, and all of us did our food and grocery shopping in that store, although I investigated the son of the owner of that store, and I carried out an investigation because he was a suspect in a different case. However, I as a customer and he, or rather, his father as the owner of this shop had a relationship that remained unchanged. I can give you many other examples where we had the most normal possible contacts, communication, irrespective of ethnicity and the work that we carried out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could you give us the identities or even names, if appropriate, of professional people who were Albanians that you regularly associated with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had colleagues who worked as judges in the district court. We socialised. We were family friends. We visited each other at home. This was a colleague of mine who worked with me in the investigation department, Arsan Miliju [phoen], he was there; and also Metush Latifi, another judge in the criminal court; then Judge Betici, who was a second-instance judge; and also there were other colleagues who worked on the district court while I was there but after that they became lawyers, they opened their own private law offices, and we remained friends, and there are a lot of lawyers. I really don't have to mention all of their names now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And these persons you've just named, they were working as judges in Pristina in 1999, were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Shefqet Betiqi and Arsan Miliju worked in the district court in 1999 as well; however, Metush Latifi unfortunately died before that. It just so happened that I carried out the investigation because his body was found in the apartment where he lived, so I carried out the on-site investigation. And after the post mortem was carried out, it was concluded that he died due to a heart attack, infarction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to finish up on this topic, was there also an Albanian couple for whom you served as a -- as a sort of godparent?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This happened a long time ago. This was a married couple who had no children for many years, over 20 years. The relatives of the husband insisted that he get a divorce because they couldn't have any children; however, he did not want to divorce the wife and after 20 years they got their first child, and he worked in the company where my husband worked and he was his immediate superior. It is a custom among the Albanian ethnic community that when a child is born they take the child out for the first time, and since we were so close, they asked if we could be the first family that they would visit and that's indeed what happened. And they came and visited us, and our home was the first home that their child visited, and for many, many years we went on socialising, even after they moved to the area around Pec.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Again just waiting for the transcript to catch up --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness be asked to speak slower, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before doing that, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The interpreters would be assisted, Mrs. Marinkovic, if you were able to speak a little more slowly when answering the questions. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the sake of efficiency I'll try to speak more slowly when I ask the questions as well, since I'm often guilty of that same fault.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, and just to complete that, in that account you gave us did you actually say that the couple lived in Junik?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It wasn't picked up. That clarifies it. Thank you. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could move to some specific matters under the ZKP, or the Serbian Law of Criminal Procedure, that was in place from 1998 to 1999, what was the age of majority for purposes of criminal liability under that act?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, according to the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force then and is still now, there were special provisions relating to under-age persons, minors, prescribing that a person who had committed a crime and was under the age of 18 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 14, Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- when the crime was committed cannot be criminally prosecuted. If pre-criminal proceedings are initiated, they are halted against such a person.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record that can be found at Article 453 of the criminal procedure code, which is Exhibit P1824. Ma'am, could you please tell us something about the structure of the judicial organs on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija during the period of 1998 through 1999?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In this period in Kosovo and Metohija there were five seats of district courts, namely, Pristina, Prizren, Kosovska Mitrovica, Pec, Gnjilane.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in addition to those district courts -- or strike that. With respect to those district courts, could you tell us what territories you as an investigative judge had responsibility for or jurisdiction over?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The jurisdiction of Pristina was the municipalities of Pristina, Kosovo Polje, Glogovac, Obilic, Lipljan, Urosevac, Kacanik, Djeneral Jankovic, and Novo Brdo. Let me just add that there were municipal courts in Pristina, Lipljan, and Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell us what types of cases you handled and processed as an investigative judge within the district court in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: As an investigative judge of the Pristina district court, pursuant to the rules of procedure of that court, I was assigned cases as they came in, regardless of the structure, the kind of the case, and regardless of who the injured party and the suspects were. But let me just clarify one thing regarding investigative judges. Investigative judges are not elected or appointed to that post, but in accordance with the annual schedule the president of the court in accordance with the rules of procedure, the president sets up the annual schedule for the judges, the roster for the judges, and this is how the decision is made who is going to be the investigative judge in any given year and carry out those tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, could you please tell us regarding 1998 and 1999 before the war with NATO how many investigative judges were there at the district court in Pristina as well as the national or ethnic make-up of that group of investigative judges?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in that period - and that was valid for the years before that and the same practice continued - every year there were four judges assigned to investigative tasks. In 1998 at the beginning of that year, there were three of us, three investigative judges, one Albanian, a Serbian, and myself, a Macedonian. Another Serbian judge was appointed later on, but in mid-1998, because the number of cases handled by the first-instance court increased, the president of the court appointed one of the judges to work in the first-instance -- at the first-instance level and another judge was appointed as the acting president of the municipal court in Pristina so that myself and this Albanian colleague for a while were the only investigative judges, and that state of affairs lasted until the end of 1998 when the judge from the municipal court came back and another judge was appointed so that in early 1998 there were four of us judges there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And how about after the commencement of the air campaign of NATO and the proclamation of war, did the number of investigative judges at the Pristina district court change at that point in time; and if so, how?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when NATO air-strikes began, that was on the 24th of March, 1999, a decision was made and military courts were set up, and when those military courts became operational a certain number of male colleagues went to work in military prosecutor's offices and military courts. So that an investigative judge was transferred to a military court and the Albanian colleague left Pristina and went abroad with his family so that this colleague of mine and myself, and this colleague was facing retirement; and he was not drafted into the army, we covered the whole of the ground there because some of our colleagues who had small children they had left Pristina for safety reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It would help I think if you would concentrate, please, on the particular questions because I'm certainly losing track of numbers. We have a statement, transcript, that in the early part of 1998 there were four of you working as investigative judges. Now, it doesn't seem consistent with the rest of what you said. Did you refer to a period when there were four investigative judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't understand your question. What period are you interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: End of 1998 -- sorry, the early part of 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the first part of 1998, there were three of us judges, but another judge came in as the fourth. But after a few months this judge who had come from the associated labour court was appointed the acting president of the municipal court in Pristina, and an investigative judge was assigned to the first-instance chamber by the president. So that over a period of a couple of months --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's clear now. And the other question you were asked was: Did the number of investigative judges change on the 24th of March? Now, is the answer to that yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And was that simply because one colleague went abroad?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a colleague went abroad and another colleague went to work to a military court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So were you the only investigative judge after the 24th of March?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there was another colleague who had come back from the municipal court, he had been working there as the acting president of the municipal court. But because he was about to retire, he could not work in military courts or organs because of his age and so he remained in the court and he worked with me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to follow-up on a few points there. First of all, do you know approximately when it was that your colleague would have left to join the military courts, was that immediately after the bombing, several weeks after, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, I can't give you the date because after the decision was made to establish military prosecutor's offices and courts, maybe 10 or 15 days after that, that was when it happened. So in this period before he left to work in the military court, he continued working with us on investigative tasks and he completed his cases. He attended on-site investigations. So before he left to work in the military court, there were three of us together with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And the one colleague who left the country, do you know the circumstances of his departure and had there been -- do you know the circumstances of his departure? Let's start with that question.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you about him. Although he was a district court judge, throughout the period that he worked there, he was concerned about his family and he was worried that because he had agreed to work in the district court as an investigative judge that his family might suffer because of that because members of the KLA exerted pressure on some people to reject appointments in the state institutions of the state of Serbia. In early 1999 before NATO air-strikes began, attacks on civilians, Albanian civilians, by the KLA escalated. So he was worried because of his family, and in the first few days of the air-strikes the number of attacks by the KLA increased again and he felt that he himself might be at risk. So he left with his family to keep his family safe. We helped him -- we drove him to -- a colleague of mine drove him to Skoplje and then he went abroad by plane.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And how about the case load that you had at the district court in Pristina in 1998, how did it compare with the time-period before 1998?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in 1998 a number of cases increased at a normal rate with regard to criminal cases involving all kinds of crimes, regardless of the injured party and the suspect. If we disregard the cases where -- that we investigated that involved terrorism and conspiracy to commit hostile acts. However, in 1998 the number of on-site investigations increased because the number of attacks on civilians, Albanian civilians, on Serbs increased; the number of attacks on the facilities, housing of refugees from [Realtime transcript read in error "in"] Croatia and Bosnia increased. So it would happen almost every day to have two or three on-site investigations because we from the district court in Pristina covered a large territory so that we did a lot of work in this period.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For purposes of the transcript, page 14, line 10, I believe the refugees were from Croatia and Bosnia and not in Croatia and Bosnia. And could you tell us please, ma'am, what was the case load like in 1999 leading up to but before the commencement of the NATO bombings?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Before the air-strikes began we worked -- it was business as usual. The number of attacks increased, we had to carry out the on-site investigations, but we could only do it where it was safe because in the second half of 1998 it already became quite risky to go out into the field, in particular where we had information that those areas were covered by the illegal organization, the KLA. But wherever it was possible and wherever it was safe, we did our work as usual. We were assisted by the personnel of the Ministry of the Interior who secured the site and the whole area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And just to complete the picture on this line of questioning, how would you describe the case load following the commencement of the NATO bombings all the way through the withdrawal in June of 1999?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: During the NATO air-strikes we did so much work. We had to do on-site investigations, we had to deal with the cases where people were brought in, people were suspects in other crimes, and we had a large number of cases involving the people who were in custody because of conspiracy to commit hostile acts. We did -- we had a full case load, myself and my colleague, and the number of on-site investigations increased to such an extent because NATO forces targeted civilian facilities in Pristina and the area around it. We had to go out and visit those scenes, and on the other hand the KLA members carried out their attacks and they were well-organized. We had a very large number of murders where civilians were murdered or they would have their own internal conflict. So we did more work then than we did in the whole of 1998. In the less than three months of the air-strikes, we did more on-site investigations than we did in the whole of 1998, and let alone 1997. Together with my colleagues, that was before one of my colleagues left to join a military court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And while we are at the point of the NATO -- at that time-period of the NATO bombings, I would like to show you Exhibit 1D301. You should have that in one of your binders as the first tab. This was promulgated by the federal government. What can you tell us about this document and the change or any effect that it had on your official work?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document that the federal document -- federal government promulgated after the state of war was declared in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia. It is a decree on implementing the Law on Criminal Procedure during the state of war. As regards this decree, as far as it pertains to investigations, I as an investigative judge and the organs of the Ministry of the Interior, we were authorised to carry out certain investigative actions if it was an urgent matter even without the approval and the recommendation of the district public prosecutor. Secondly, this decree also stipulated that the time -- the period of time that a person could be held in custody in pre-trial proceedings and or pre-investigative proceedings and during the investigation in accordance with the criminal procedure act a person that was arrested could be detained in custody for a maximum of 72 hours. After that time-period a person had to be brought before an investigative judge. According to this decree, the personnel of the Ministry of the Interior could, if a person -- if a criminal report was filed against a person for an act of terrorism, this person could be held for a maximum of 30 days. You can see that from Article 8 of this decree. This decree also cut short the dead-lines for the service of the indictment to the accused and also cut short the dead-line by which the accused could file motions alleging defects in the indictment. So this made it easier for the courts to proceed, given the conditions in which we worked because the state of war was already in force and there was a huge number of cases that had to be dealt with and the investigative judges and the Ministry of the Interior, the public prosecutor's offices, we all had a huge amount of work to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, and if I can just remind you to try to slow down, especially when we're reading the law so that the translators can keep up with us. And did this -- did this decision have an effect on the abilities of the organs of the interior to conduct -- to conduct on-site investigations on their own in urgent cases as well?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This decree -- let me just have a look --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Would that be Article 6?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Article 6, Article 6, paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned at some point in time there was the establishment of the military court system on the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. Prior to that time were the civil judiciary organs the only ones that were available to do investigations and on-site investigations?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Before military courts and prosecutor's offices were established and before they started working, it was the investigating judge who went out into the field to carry out on-site investigations. If he could not do so, then he would authorise organs of the interior to do that. And in urgent cases, organs of the Ministry of the Interior could carry out an on-site investigation on their own as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you going to be looking at the time-scale of this? I take it there was a military court system prior to 1999, at least I thought that was the evidence so far, and that there was a separate one or different one established for the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe my question asked about the one that had been established on the territory of Kosovo-Metohija -- I thought I had said during the war, but I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Is this military court system we're talking about the one that was established at the time of the NATO bombings, the war with NATO, or what -- did it exist prior to that time, Madam?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, military courts and prosecutor's offices existed before the state of war as well, but at that time, military courts had certain territorial jurisdiction. On the basis of the Law on Courts and Prosecutor's Offices, their jurisdiction was regulated too. When the state of war was declared, courts started functioning in a different way. Beforehand, the military courts in Pristina were not actually located in Pristina. There was a military court in Nis that included the territory of Pristina as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You will have to slow down for the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. The earlier answer at line 17 on page 17, I don't know what it refers to, but it doesn't seem to me to matter. However, if you do -- if it is important to know the position before there ever were military courts, if there was such a time in the recent past, then you need to clarify it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I will do that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, following the commencement of the NATO air-strikes but prior to the Pristina military court and prosecutor's office getting up and running, who handled investigations and on-site investigations on that territory?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, before the NATO bombing started in the territory of Pristina, where the district court had its jurisdiction, on-site investigations were carried out by the investigating judges of the district court, whereas the municipal court had its own investigative judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Following the NATO bombing, following the commencement of the bombing, did that same system stay in place until the military courts in -- and prosecutor's office in Pristina became active and up and running?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: During the state of war we continued carrying out our duties in line with our jurisdiction, as was the case until then; however, our work was impeded due to the NATO bombing. As for jurisdiction is concerned, we really didn't have anything to do with the military courts. Their jurisdiction was quite different. So we continued working irrespective of whether or when military courts were established in the territory of Serbia. Now, if we carried out an on-site investigation and if we found an NN corpse, after the post mortem it is established that it was a case of violent death, say caused by a fire-arm, and later on it is established who the perpetrator of the said crime was, and perhaps if it is established that the perpetrator was a military person then the criminal complaint is sent to the military court along with the evidence collected in the pre-trial proceedings like this on-site investigation, the record of the on-site investigation, the post mortem, so that the military court could afterwards take over the case and continue proceedings against that particular person. Was that the point of your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think that explains most of it, and I thank you for slowing down. I know it's difficult to try and keep the pace under control. Trust me, I've had that difficulty for a long time in this courtroom, so you're not alone. Could you tell us what your official workday and time of on-call duty was like as an investigative judge for both the periods before and during the air war with NATO?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the investigating judge had to be on duty as well. When there were four of us investigative judges, each one of us was on duty for a week during the course of one month. From one Monday to the next Monday, 24 hours a day. Everything that happened within the course of that week, irrespective of whether it was an on-site investigation or bringing persons into custody, all of that was handled by the duty judge. When there were only two of us left, then our tour of duty would be 15 days a month. During the NATO bombing, we could no longer follow that schedule because we had to go out into the field a lot, so my colleague and I tried to work out an arrangement who would be free when one would be working on regular cases and the other one would go out for on-site investigations. So we really did not pay much attention to working hours. We just wanted to get the work done because that's what the situation was like.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now focusing on the time-period in 1999 during the NATO war, what types of on-site investigations did you undertake, that is to say what types of occurrences did you conduct on-site investigations for, if you could give us an overview?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, during the NATO bombing, we carried out on-site investigations because NATO targeted and bombed civilian facilities. So my colleague carried out an on-site investigation when the post office building was hit and the institute for retirement insurance, private homes were hit then as well. I carried out an on-site investigation in the neighbourhood of Grmija, where a civilian building had been hit. It was a recreation centre. The guard of that sports facility was killed and the building itself was razed to the ground. Nothing was left. My colleague, before he went to the military court, carried out an on-site investigation because a NATO bomb had hit in the area of Lipljan, a hunting area. In Lipljan, I carried out this on-site investigation because in the village of Staro Gradsko, cluster bombs hit private homes. There were casualties, fatalities, a little girl was killed, an old man, and there were two persons who were wounded. We found many cluster bombs out in the fields, so we called the military investigative organs to help out because they were well-versed in such matters, that is to say how these cluster bombs should be removed from the fields. In addition to these on-site investigations, we also worked on homicides because in some areas NN bodies were found by the road or houses, we tried to identify them and to establish the cause of death. Records were kept of all of this, photographs were taken, post mortem orders were issued, and cases were filed in relation to these occurrences. Since we could not be everywhere at all the places where on-site investigations were supposed to be carried out, after the organs of the Ministry of the Interior would inform me about what had happened on the ground, I would agree with them that sometimes they would carry out the on-site investigation on their own because we simply did not have enough time to complete an on-site investigation everywhere. After the on-site investigation, the organs of the Ministry of the Interior would provide information to me and the prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in addition to doing investigations and on-site inspections for NATO bombing, civilian damage -- civilian casualties, killings or murders or deaths, did you also have occasion to do on-site investigations for damage to property or for theft, et cetera, regular types of criminal occurrences?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in relation to these regular criminal occurrences, we did not carry out on-site investigations. We pursued requests to carry out an investigation that were filed by the prosecutor after the organs of the Ministry of the Interior had reported to them. During the NATO bombing, I carried out on-site investigations in cases of homicide too.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to more of the specifics of actual investigations, but first of all I'd like to ask you a general question, generally speaking, is the mere fact that an on-site investigation takes place mean that the occurrence is always classifiable in the end as a criminal act or transgression? For a reminder, I think you mentioned the instance of one of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, since we go out to the site and since the investigation takes place, all the material evidence is collected there and then. It doesn't mean that a crime had been committed by virtue of that fact and that we know who the perpetrator was, if indeed it was a crime. In relation to this, I want to say the following: We went out for on-site investigations when homicides took place and when suicides took place, when people hanged themselves, when people used fire-arms or hunting guns to commit suicide. After a post mortem is carried out and after it is established what the cause of death is, there is no further work on that particular case to see who the possible perpetrator was in case it is established that it wasn't a suicide. I mentioned the case when my colleague's body was found in his own apartment. After the on-site investigation in agreement with the forensic pathologist, a post mortem was carried out and it was established that he died due to a heart attack because he had been a heart patient before that too. So we were not suspicious, either we as the court or his family. We did not continue an investigation on this case. We did not look into the possibility of it -- of his death having been the result of a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you mentioned that in addition to on-site investigations both you and your colleague undertook other work as well. What other types of work were part of your duties as an investigative judge within the system in Pristina?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as an investigative judge, I worked on cases where the authorised prosecutor had filed a request for an on-site investigation. Perpetrators and injured parties were of different ethnic backgrounds, starting with homicides, abuse of office, theft, at first this was under district courts all the way up to crimes of terrorism, conspiracy to commit hostile acts. That is to say all kinds of cases that were within our line of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In addition to on-site investigations, did you also conduct interviews and other court business during the day?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I did regular work in relation to regular cases. If on that day suspects were to be heard, witnesses as well, if I was not on duty then I would do my regular work in relation to investigation cases and my colleague who would be on duty would go out on on-site investigations. During working hours we would go out on on-site investigations, but we did it in the afternoon, during the night, at midnight, depending on when the particular occurrence took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And under -- under whose jurisdiction are exhumations and autopsies or corpse inspections?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Obduction [Realtime transcript read in error "abduction"] and exhumations are exclusively within the remit of the investigative judge. It is the investigative judge who is to issue an order if he or she believes that an obduction is to be performed. Obduction were performed by the Institute of Forensic Medicine. Obduction were always carried out if there was something suspicious about the death involved and if the court or forensic pathologist cannot rule out that possibility or if he cannot establish the cause of death on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us the steps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment, Mr. Ivetic. I wonder if the interpreter could assist. The word abduction has been used on at least two occasions in the transcript, and I think I heard the word, it's not just a transcript. Can you clarify that whether --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Until now we used the word "post mortem." Then Mr. Ivetic used the word "obduction," and that is why we then in the answer used the word "obduction" too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think he used that word.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: O-B-D is the spelling. I now see the transcript I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a word I'm not familiar with. It's something I'm not familiar with. Is there such a thing as an obduction?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In Serbian there's an "obdukcija."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In English we use the word post mortem, interpreter's note, but Mr. Ivetic now used the word "obd," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: None in English?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No, I think the -- just let me double check. I used the term exhumations, autopsies and corpse inspections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I see, I see. It's this problem of using two languages again, Mr. Ivetic. If you used the Serb word which is what the interpreter is saying, then that may have caused the difficulty, but how should we read obduction here, is it autopsy?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I did not use the Serb word I spoke in complete English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's what I though, but has caused a measure of confusion. But, in any event we were talking about both autopsies and corpse inspections I think. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it may be the word corpse inspection or the two words corpse inspection that caused the difficulty. Anyway, let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think we did have prior evidence from one witness explaining the difference from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, there are cases -- I understand it where it's not possible for a full post mortem to be carried out and the corpse is inspected as far as is reasonably possible on site. So please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Madam, if you could tell us the -- describe for us the typical steps and procedure for both an on-site investigation and, indeed, an official investigation including an explanation of the point where the work jurisdiction and authority of the police and the investigative judge ends.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one thing. What is carried out on site is only investigation, investigation is on-site investigation, corpse inspection, or exhumation. The authorised prosecutor then takes further action for a complete post mortem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And could you explain for us the steps leading up to such an investigation and define for us the point in time when the authority and obligations of police on the one hand and the investigative judge on the other hand cease and then who -- who -- what organ continues to have authority in the situation beyond that?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The organ of the interior files a criminal complaint with the authorised prosecutor if there is a suspicion that the suspected person had committed a crime. The public prosecutor, when receiving this criminal complaint, makes his own assessment on the basis of the information contained in the criminal complaint, whether that is sufficient for him to continue proceedings, or rather, to have a request for carrying out an investigation with the investigative judge. If the criminal complaint does not contain sufficient information, then the prosecutor in charge has the authority to ask the organs of the interior to collect additional information, which the organ of the interior is duty-bound to do within a reasonable period of doubt -- reasonable period of time and then the prosecutor receives this information. The request for an investigation can be made, but then the prosecutor can also reject the criminal complaint if there are not sufficient grounds for carrying out an investigation against a particular person. If the public prosecutor accepts this criminal complaint and does file a request to carry out an investigation, after the request for investigation the organs of the interior no longer have any authority whatsoever or influence over the court and the prosecutor's office. The only thing that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior do in the process of investigation is to carry out some specific work within investigation. Or if the suspect does not respond to a subpoena or summons, then the investigative judge can subpoena him actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And some follow-up questions on that. At page 27, line 15 to 16 were you're quoted as saying that: "The only thing that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: "Within investigation," is that were always suspect to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, the transcript is incomplete because you were speaking very quickly, again I think probably because you're reading from something. Could you try to slow down when you do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But also repeat that quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At page 27, lines 14 through 17 actually, you're recorded as saying that: "The only thing that the organs of the Ministry of the Interior do in the process of investigation is to carry out some specific work within investigation." Is that work always subject upon a specific request or direction from the relevant prosecutor with authority over the matter?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the relevant organs of the Ministry of the Interior in the pre-criminal proceedings before they file a criminal complaint to the prosecutor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. I'm certain that your answer related to the situation after the prosecutor had decided that -- to accept the complaint and proceed with the investigation, and it's after that stage that we're concerned about. You say that the role of the Ministry of the Interior is very limited, and it's that role at that stage that Mr. Ivetic is asking about.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After the public prosecutor files a request for an investigation with the investigative judge in terms of a specific crime and against a particular person, in relation to that case the organs of the Ministry of the Interior have nothing to do after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And am I correct that at that point in time the investigative judge upon the authority of the prosecutor carries the investigation and may request assistance of the organs of the interior but not in all circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you explain for us the interaction between the investigative judge and the organs of the Ministry of the Interior upon the acceptance of a criminal denunciation and the commencement of an investigation upon that criminal denunciation.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Once the investigative judge receives the request for investigation filed by the public prosecutor, the investigative judge may authorise the organs of the Ministry of the Interior to carry out certain investigative actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, you also mentioned that the prosecutor may accept or reject a criminal denunciation. Does any -- first of all, does any organ of the Ministry of the Interior or any other body have any influence or legal effect on the public prosecutor in this regard or is it their pure discretion?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Once the public prosecutor receives the criminal report, that person is the -- has the sole authority and has the discretion to decide whether to accept the criminal report, to what extent, whether to return it for amendment and whether to file a criminal proceedings -- to institute criminal proceedings based on the investigative -- the results of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And does the relevant prosecutor at that point in time also have the discretion to reject and not act upon a criminal denunciation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you'll need to begin that question again because you were speaking over the translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In those circumstances, does the relevant prosecutor have the right and discretion to reject and not proceed upon a criminal denunciation without even giving a rationale or reason for the same?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The public prosecutor does have the authority under the Law on Criminal Procedure that when he receives a criminal report and when he deems that there are no grounds for a request for investigation to be filed or if there are no grounds for suspicion based on the criminal report that a person had committed a criminal offence to reject such criminal report; and he may or may need not inform the organ of the Ministry of the Interior or any person that actually filed the criminal report of this development. The only thing that he's duty-bound to do, if there is an injured party in that case, he must inform the injured party if he believes that there are grounds for this person to file a legal suit against the suspect on his own.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for purposes of clarity, Your Honours, I've noticed -- I've been using the word criminal denunciation, which is the term that I was told by CLSS is the official translation of "krivicna prijava," the Serbian word. Criminal report and criminal complaint have been used in the transcript. As far as I'm concerned they mean the same thing and they're both -- they're all legitimate translations, but that way if someone's following in the transcript, that's the same -- the same instrument that we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Judge Marinkovic, you've told us --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There are two issues there. I think you've said that you do not require to -- the prosecutor does not require to tell the Ministry of the Interior official reporting the matter of a decision not to accept the criminal denunciation. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And are you also saying that having made a decision the prosecutor does not require to record any reason for that decision anywhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Once the public prosecutor decides to reject the criminal report, he drafts an official note for that case, stating the reasons why the criminal report was rejected. And if the person that actually filed the criminal report wants to find out, he may address the public prosecutor and ask. But the public prosecutor is under no obligation to inform the organs of the Ministry of the Interior. He may do so, but he need not, I think it's Article 151, 2, of the law on criminal procedure.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The official term for "krivicna prijava" is criminal report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You identify a person there as the person that actually filed the criminal report. Will that be a person from the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So who do you -- who do you mean by the person that actually filed the criminal report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When an organ of the Ministry of the Interior files the criminal report - well, that would depend on the actual crime, there is an injured party, if it is a homicide, it is the family; if it is abuse of office, then it would be a company; if it is a theft or robbery, then we have a natural person that is the injured party. And in such a case when the public prosecutor decides to reject a criminal report, he is under an obligation pursuant to Article 61, paragraph 2 of the Law on Criminal Procedure to inform the injured party of the fact that the criminal report was rejected and to inform the injured party that within eight days this person may institute criminal proceedings against the person who committed -- allegedly committed the act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I would need a little clarification here. You said that when the report is rejected by the prosecutor and he's informed of this fact, he can institute criminal proceedings against the persons who committed. What do you mean by that? I mean, is there a matter going -- I mean taking an impression from the prosecutor and filing a case in the court directly or you want to say something else? I couldn't get this, line 15, 16, 17 of what you have said. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you mean cases involving injured parties, once an injured party is informed by the public prosecutor, the injured party has a right to file a request for an investigation with the investigative judge, subsidiary prosecutor or plaintiff, the subsidiary plaintiff or an injured party as a plaintiff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, is this a suitable time to interrupt your examination or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It could be in five minutes. I did have another question that I wanted to try and get in before the break, but it's not -- it's not precisely on the same topic, it's taking a step further so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I understand Mr. Hannis has some administrative issues and we might find out what these are before we have the break, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, we will have a break shortly, as is the normal practice here. We're going to interrupt your evidence a bit earlier than the break so that we can deal with administrative matters. We will be resuming about ten minutes to 11.00, so could you please leave the courtroom with the usher and we'll see you again when we resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, one matter, can I ask the usher to give her her classes in case she needs them for reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, you had certain matters you wished to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. Yes. The first matter related to some photographs that we used with the Witness Dragan Milenkovic last week. Some of those photographs were under seal in connection with an earlier witness in the Prosecution case. That under seal had to do with the connection with that witness. We think it's appropriate to lift the seal on three of the photos we used with Milenkovic last week, those being Exhibits P2627, P2628, and P2630, and I'd make an oral application to do that at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I see no one resisting that application, so we will authorise that, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Related to that matter, Your Honour, Mr. Ivetic raised the point that when the protected witness had testified earlier in the case in connection with those photos, there was an issue that one of those photos had been published in Danas, and Mr. Ivetic raised some concerns at that time in, I think, February 2007 about a leak relating to protected witnesses. You inquired of me if there had been any investigation done. From what I've been able to determine, Your Honour, it appears that if -- there was nothing in violation of the Court order. We had a pending motion for protective measures for that witness testifying at that time, but there was no leak from the OTP. A private individual who had possession of those photos may have been likely to have been in the loop that led to those photographs being published in Danas, but he was not a witness who testified here, and he was not subject to any protective measures that were in place in connection with it. So as far as I've been able to determine, there was no violation of any Court order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was that person someone who was likely to be aware of the application for protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does that not give rise to concern?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if I'm going to have any further discussion about this. I probably should do it in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, before considering it any further, I will need to remind myself of the circumstances in which it arose before, which I'll do when we have the break. And it may be that if anything else is to be said on this, we can deal with it immediately after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The third thing I wanted to raise is in connection with P948, which is the interview with General Lukic. Mr. Fila, I think, is the only one who has responded so far identifying portions of that interview that he proposed. We have some further translation of. I raise the issue, Your Honour, because I was thinking about in terms of a practical matter for CLSS. The transcript we have, we have -- someone has listened to the audio and we have B/C/S transcript and English transcript intermixed. I don't -- there's not any further translation to be done. What CLSS could do, I suppose, is comment on and say that B/C/S that is spoken there is not quite a full, accurate translation of what was said in the English, which as you understand in a simultaneous translation, as we have in the courtroom --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- may happen. But I'm not sure what CLSS's job is to do, is to make some commentaries or to prepare a separate report. I'm asking for some guidance from the Court on how we would proceed on that and what's going to be most helpful to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the transcription you're talking about one compiled by the Prosecution, by your own office?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And would it not, in fact, be compiled from listening -- or it wouldn't be done by listening to the tape. It's simply a transcription of the interpreter's translation at the time, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I believe it was done by watching and listening to the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But done by your office?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, by language assistants in our office.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But -- but the questions would be asked in English, translated into B/C/S, the answer would be B/C/S and translated into English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would that not be done at the time and simply transcribed automatically so that there's no translation being done by the person transcribing it, they're simply writing or typing up what they hear on the tape?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Right. And in that situation, Mr. Fila is saying that perhaps some of it needs to be revised for accuracy. Now, I would be inclined to think that the principle of ensuring that justice is seen to be done in a situation where the OTP compile the document demands that where there's some sort of challenge that that should be reviewed by an independent body, CLSS falls into that category, and if parties can responsibly identify the passages that really need that exercise done, then in our view that should be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Mr. Fila has --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you require us to order that to be done, then we will have to consider an application that identifies the areas in which the matter is required; if, on the other hand, you can between yourselves arrange to identify these areas and make a submission to CLSS, that would be ideal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Fila has done so, and I'm prepared to send that over now and ask for those portions to be done, but I don't want to send that over and next week get something from somebody else. I would like to have a cut-off time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's have the cut-off point at close of business on Tuesday, and then it can be submitted, and anyone else who has anything to raise should raise it then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It does raise the issue, of course, of the timing of this. Mr. Ivetic, is it likely that Mr. Lukic will give evidence? Just a moment, Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We -- we at this point do plan to -- we have him on the list and we haven't made the final decision yet. As so he's on the list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If he is to give evidence, then the timing of this becomes important.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We would, of course, wait until that's done I think to call him if indeed he were to testify. That would I think be the logical route to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that I did what I could in the most accurate and the fastest possible terms, and I abided by what Mr. Hannis said not to translate the very beginning, although it is quite interesting because there Philip Coo is presented as an investigator of the OTP, not an analyst. This is -- I found it quite interesting, but that's water under the bridge now. But what I listed here are where I see the differences in the terminology, in the way in which questions are asked in Serbian, what is translated into English, so the only accurate picture is when we hear everything that is said in English and in Serbian and I never asked for any translation to be done. So that I think that I really did all I could to keep it very brief and clear and the Lukic Defence could not respond because they have so much work to do. So I did it for everyone just to save time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So are you satisfied everyone has commented so far as they may wish?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We may have one or more -- I noticed I think one additional section that I saw that had a difference between the translation and the -- the English and the B/C/S. I will do that by the close of business Tuesday, as the Court has instructed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is involved here is simply identifying passages which CLSS will be invited to revise the translation of. It's as simple as that, and if there are arguments then to be made about what was actually meant by what was said then these are for later in the proceedings or for examination of witnesses as we pass through the trial. We'll take our break now -- sorry, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just to assist you, Your Honours, since you said you wanted to inform ourselves about the situation Mr. Hannis raised about the photographs in the Danas paper, since there are several days of testimony. I think the discussion that's pertinent to some, the 31st of January, 2007, but at the tail end of that day before the witness actually testified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, to look more closely at that issue will take me longer than a 20-minute break, I'm afraid. So it will be given further consideration, and if any further address is required from you or anyone else, then we'll notify you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. So we can resume the evidence now with Mrs. Marinkovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mrs. Marinkovic, thank you for your patience. We can now continue with the evidence. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we had left off -- you had explained to us where the authority of the MUP ended with respect to an investigation. Can you explain for us what the steps are and what happens to a case when you as the investigating judge complete your work.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When I, as an investigative judge, received a request for investigation, the first thing I check is whether I have jurisdiction, whether the request for investigation contains all the relevant data, including the personal details of the suspect, the factual description of the crime, and then I set a hearing date at which the suspect is questioned. When the suspect is questioned, and if I find that there are grounds for the investigation to continue, I, as the investigative judge, I issue a decision for an investigation. If I disagree with a request for the investigation filed by the competent prosecutor, I, as an investigative judge, am authorised to express my disagreement with the request for an investigation and then the chamber, relevant chamber, of the court rules in chambers on this request. If I decide that an investigation is in place, I gather all the information, all the data, in my investigation that make it possible to draw a conclusion whether the suspect did, indeed, commit the crime he is charged with. In the investigation phase I gather the evidence designated by the prosecutor in the request for investigation, and as an investigative judge I'm authorised to gather other evidence if I deem it necessary to come to the material truth or the objective truth. Once the investigation is complete, I submit the file, the case file, to the public prosecutor, who then proceeds.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at that stage where you submit the file, the case file, to the public prosecutor who then proceeds, does the Serbian MUP have any influence, role, or authority at that stage of the proceedings either?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, during the course of the investigation, that is to say before the case file is presented to the public prosecutor for eventual indictment and proceedings, under what circumstances can an investigative judge under the criminal procedure code of Serbia limit access to defence counsel to documents and information out of security concerns?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: After I issue a decision for an investigation, the defence counsel or defence counsel teams, if there are several accused, have the right to inspect the case file and any items or objects that are the object of the crime. But in exceptional circumstances in the previous preliminary stages of the proceedings before the indictment is issued if there are grounds to do so and in the interests of the defence and the security of the state, I as an investigative judge can issue a decision preventing the defence counsel from inspecting the case file and the objects or items in this case. The defence counsel have the right to appeal against this decision to the judges who will then rule in chambers if they deem that any other rights, apart from this right, has been violated, the right to inspect the case file. They are entitled to file a complaint to the president of the court against me, against my work.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I could ask you this initial appeal that you said is heard by judges, how many judges would hear such an appeal?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear your question. I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Where you say the defence counsel have a right to appeal against a decision to the judges who will then rule in chambers, how many judges would comprise that body that would rule in chambers on any appeal by defence counsel in this regard?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: This chamber, it's a panel, a three-judge panel, they are professional judges and they deal with any appeals that have to do with the investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the next question I have for you. Thank you. And the next question that I have for you: Would such a restriction on access to documents and information continue after the investigation is complete and an indictment issues?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: No. This is a temporary measure during the investigation. Once the indictment has been issued the defence counsel have ample time after receiving the indictment to prepare for their defence, to inspect the case file, and to await trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now if you could please tell us what in essence is a criminal denunciation, in Serbian "krivicna privaja," what is contained in it, who can prepare and submit such instruments, and under what conditions?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: A criminal report is a document that actually initiates a criminal proceedings. It must contain information about the person who is listed there as the perpetrator of the crime. It must contain a factual description of the crime for which there are grounds for suspicion that a person named in the criminal report actually committed it and the legal qualification of the crime. It also must state what data or what evidence possibly led to this knowledge, all of that must be appended to the criminal report. Apart from the organs of the Ministry of the Interior who file criminal reports for crimes that must be prosecuted ex officio, criminal reports may be filed by other institutions of the state and by citizens, natural persons. Every citizen has the right to file a criminal report. Citizens may file criminal reports directly with the public prosecutor or with the organs of the Ministry of the Interior. Criminal reports are filed only when there are grounds for suspicion that a certain person committed a certain crime, and a criminal report may also be filed against persons unknown if we know what the crime was, but at that time it is not known, and it is impossible to determine or to identify the perpetrator.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, according to the relevant provisions of the criminal procedure code that was in effect at the time in 1999, what were the legal obligations and responsibilities of all citizens of the state in regards to reporting criminal acts and criminal perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: In the Law on Criminal Procedure there is an article stipulating that every person who comes upon a perpetrator in the course of the perpetration of the crime is under an obligation to arrest this person and hand this person over, either to the investigative judge or to the organ -- to an organ of the Ministry of the Interior. As far as I can recall now, the article in question is Article 191, paragraph 4 of the Law on Criminal Procedure that was in force at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And again for the record, the relevant exhibit is P1824, where Article 191, subpart 4, can be found. Madam, did this obligation continue to exist during the proclamation of the state of war?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And could you tell us in terms of the persons who all was covered by this legal obligation of reporting crimes and/or perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the term that is used in this article, anybody or everybody, it covers police officers, authorised officials, soldiers, ordinary citizens, so anybody who comes upon a person in the commission of a crime is under an obligation to arrest that person. That's the wording.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Am I correct that there is also an obligation then to report it either to the organs of the interior or to the judicial organs?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What were the legal ramifications of someone's failure to so report a criminal act and/or knowledge of a criminal perpetrator?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: The Law on Criminal Procedure in Serbia describes the crime of failure to report a perpetrator, failure to report a crime, and in the relevant article, the criminal sanctions are envisaged for any person that fails to report a crime or to report a perpetrator of a crime. But in this article it is also stated - I think it is paragraph 2 of Article 203 - that if an authorised official fails to report a perpetrator in the course of the performance of their duty, then the punishment is more severe than the one envisaged in paragraph 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And for the record, Exhibit P1020 has Article 203 of the Criminal Code of the Republic of Serbia. I have a notation that it's page 63, I believe that in the Serbian. I don't have a notation for the English. Madam, when organs of the -- when organs of internal affairs bring a criminal denunciation to the public prosecutor, is that prosecutor bound to follow the exact qualification of the criminal act as set forth in the police criminal denunciation?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: When the public prosecutor receives a criminal report filed by an organ of the Ministry of the Interior, he is not under an obligation to retain the legal qualification of the crime. He is authorised on the basis of the factual description of the crime contained in the criminal report to give a different legal qualification if he believes that the act itself constitutes a different crime from that that is listed or alleged in the criminal report.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like to return to your work. Did you have occasion in the course of your work to conduct investigations against -- regarding suspects and victims of all ethnicities and nationalities without any preference or bias?

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like a take a moment to look at some.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit 6D140 up on the screen, the first page will suffice for now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Madam, we have a document here on the screen. Could you please tell us what -- first of all, what kind of document this is once we get it back up on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a criminal report --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just one second --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. The exhibit is under seal, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I think I recall the circumstances of that. It was in relation to the testimony of a certain witness with regard to a third party.

utterances.speaker: MS. CARTER
utterances.text: Respectfully, Your Honour, I believe I may be of assistance. This exhibit was referred to in the context of the testimony of Aleksandar Vasiljevic. It was actually in relation -- he was being questioned on another case and which he reported on, and that specific paragraph was being -- it was redacted from his statement itself. So this generally relates, because it's talking about the same time-period; however, it isn't exactly what Mr. Vasiljevic was speaking to. So I see no problem in lifting the seal as to this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We shall lift the seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And thank you, Madam Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Judge Marinkovic, if you could please tell us first of all what kind of document is this that we have before us.

utterances.speaker: DANICA MARINKOVIC
